## Öne konan ve ardında bıraktığı

Türk okuru tercih fiilinin kökünü aslında tanır. "Eser", "âsâr", "tesir" hep bu köktendir. "Eser" bugün daha çok sanat ya da yazı ürününü anlatır. Ama "ortada eseri yok" derken eski anlamı, yani izi hâlâ yaşar. Arapçada kökün bu yüzü açıktır: {ar:الأثر بقية ما يرى من كل شيء وما لا يرى بعد أن تبقى فيه علقة, tr:el-eserü bakıyyetü mâ yürâ min külli şey' ve mâ lâ yürâ ba'de en tebkâ fîhi ulka, gloss:eser, her şeyin görünen ya da görünmeyip bir ilişiği kalan artığıdır, source:"ء ث ر,B003"}. Yara izi de böyle anlatılırdı: {ar:الأثر من الجرح وغيره في الجسد يبرأ ويبقى أثره, tr:el-eserü mine'l-cürhi ve ğayrihî fi'l-ceset, yebrau ve yebkâ eseruh, gloss:bedendeki yara iyileşir, izi kalır, source:"ء ث ر,B003"}. Öne koymak ile iz bırakmak aynı köktedir. Bu iki anlamı birbirine bağlayan şey, ayetin söylediği bir şey değil, bir yorumdur. Ama kök bu yorumu çağırır: ne öne konursa geride bir iz bırakır.

İzler yerde kalmıştır, onları bırakanlar ise alınıp götürülmüştür. Geride kalan iz, sahibini korumamıştır.

Kökün bir kullanımı bunu somut bir aletle gösterir. Deve sahipleri devenin tabanını bir demirle işaretlerdi: {ar:المئثرة حديدة يؤثر بها خف البعير ليعرف أثره في الأرض, tr:el-mi'sera hadîdetün yü'serü bihâ huffü'l-baîri li-yu'rafe eseruhû fi'l-ard, gloss:mi'sera, devenin tabanına iz basılan demirdir; böylece yerdeki izi tanınır, source:"ء ث ر,B008"}. Bu işin nasıl yapıldığı da anlatılır: {ar:الأثرة أن يسحى باطن خف البعير بحديدة وتلك الحديدة مئثرة, tr:el-üsretü en yüshâ bâtınü huffi'l-baîri bi-hadîde ve tilke'l-hadîdetü mi'sera, gloss:üsre, devenin tabanının iç yüzünün bir demirle kazınmasıdır; o demire mi'sera denir, source:"ء ث ر,B008"}. Aletin işi şöyledir: işaret tabanın altındadır, deve onu göremez. Ama attığı her adımda kumda kendine özgü bir iz kalır. Kaybolan ya da çalınan deveyi sahibi o izden bulur. Ayetin yanında bu alet şunu duyurur: insanın öne koyduğu şey adımlarının altına basılır. Kişi izini kendisi görmez, ama yürüdüğü yol onu ele verir. Birinci ayetteki "ad" ile on ikinci ayetteki "ateş" kelimelerinde de bir damga yankılanır. Bu damga sahnesi surenin bütününe aittir. Bu ayetin kelimesi ona tabanın altındaki demiri katar.

## Aktarılan söz

Kökün bir yüzü daha surenin sonuna doğru açılır. Bir sözü başkasından nakletmek de bu fiille söylenirdi: {ar:أثرت الحديث إذا ذكرته عن غيرك وحديث مأثور, tr:esertü'l-hadîse izâ zekertehû an ğayrike ve hadîsün me'sûr, gloss:bir sözü başkasından aktardığında esertü denir; aktarılagelen söze me'sûr denir, source:"ء ث ر,B002"}. Bir insanın anlatılagelen güzel işlerine de bu kökten ad verilirdi: {ar:المآثر ما يروى من مكارم الإنسان, tr:el-meâsiru mâ yürvâ min mekârimi'l-insân, gloss:measir, insanın anlatılagelen değerli işleridir, source:"ء ث ر,B002"}. Bir insan öldükten sonra ondan anlatılan şey, hayattayken neyi öne koyduğudur.

## Yakın olan hayat

Türkçede "dünya" bir isimdir: üzerinde yaşadığımız küre, haritası ve coğrafyası olan bir yer. Ayette ise {ar:ٱلدُّنْيَا, tr:ed-dünyâ, gloss:daha yakın olan, source:87:16} hayatı niteleyen bir sıfattır: "daha yakın" anlamındaki edna'nın dişil biçimidir. "El-hayâtü'd-dünyâ" sözü kelimesi kelimesine "yakın hayat", "berideki hayat" demektir. Adın nedenini Araplar açıkça söylerdi: {ar:سميت الدنيا لدنوها, tr:sümmiyeti'd-dünyâ li-dünüvvihâ, gloss:dünyâya yakınlığından ötürü bu ad verildi, source:"د ن و,B002"}. Bu yüzden kelime her zaman bir "uzak" olanı gerektirir. Bir yer bildirmez, bir mesafe bildirir. Türkçedeki "dünya" bu karşılaştırmayı artık taşımaz. Ayetteki kelime ise ancak yanında bir ötesi bulunduğu için yakındır.

Aynı söz başka surelerde de geçer {source:23:37} {source:45:24}. Ötesi olmadığını söyleyenler bile hayatlarına "daha yakın olan" adını verir. Câsiye suresi bu söz için şöyle der: {ar:وَمَا لَهُم بِذَٰلِكَ مِنْ عِلْمٍ, tr:ve mâ lehüm bi-zâlike min ilm, gloss:bu konuda hiçbir bilgileri yoktur, source:45:24}.

+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.12.25	loving life in this world and eternal life	Jesus says that loving one's life loses it, while giving up one's life in this world keeps it for eternal life. It is an unusually direct Christian formulation of the commentary's preference for near life versus enduring life.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.18.22	possessions, the poor, and treasure in heaven	When the ruler asks about eternal life, Jesus tells him to give possessions to the poor, have treasure in heaven, and follow. It joins the commentary's chief-place language to its augment about wealth withheld from the needy.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.33	almsgiving and an unfailing heavenly treasure	Jesus connects giving alms with purses that do not wear out and treasure in heaven. It supplies a concrete reversal of the commentary's worldly self-allocation: what is given away becomes the enduring possession.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.34	treasure and the heart	Jesus locates the heart where treasure is. This directly illuminates the commentary's claim that preference is a love that gives its object the place of honor, not a detached calculation.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.16	God alone possessing immortality	God alone possesses immortality in this doxology. It gives a direct Christian formulation to the commentary's claim that permanence cannot finally be reserved by creatures for themselves.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.17	uncertain riches and hope in God	The rich are told not to set hope on uncertain wealth but on God. As the immediate context of the already relevant future foundation, it identifies the false object of confidence in the commentary's preference scene.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.3.17	wealthy self-sufficiency and unseen poverty	Laodicea claims to be rich and in need of nothing while not recognizing its wretched, poor, blind, and naked state. Its diagnosis of wealth's self-deception gives a counterpoint to the commentary's claim that wrong ordering may survive apparent knowledge.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.4.17	momentary affliction and eternal glory	Momentary, light affliction produces an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison. It supplies a precise temporal reversal for the commentary's contrast between a present cost and what endures.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.7.31	using the world as its form passes away	Those who use the world are instructed not to use it as though it were final, because its present form passes away. This closely fits the commentary's distinction between having a share in the near life and enthroning it.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.4.14	life as a passing mist	James calls human life a mist that appears briefly and then vanishes. It directly sharpens the commentary's discussion of long life, the appointed end, and the inability to make near life remain.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.45	neglect of the least and final judgment	Failure to serve the hungry, stranger, naked, sick, and imprisoned is treated as failure to serve the Son of Man. It gives the commentary's orphan-and-poor augment an explicitly eschatological test of what one has put first.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.46	eternal punishment and eternal life	The final separation ends in eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other. It gives the lasting consequence that frames the commentary's contrast of the near life with the life beyond.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Heb.11.24	Moses refusing Pharaoh's household	Moses refuses to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. This distinct first step in Hebrews' Moses sequence gives the commentary's choice of honor and chief place a direct courtly setting.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Heb.11.27	Moses not fearing the king's anger	Moses leaves Egypt without fearing the king's anger and perseveres as though seeing the unseen. It closely accompanies the commentary's Pharaoh scene, contrasting a visible ruler's force with an unseen but decisive reality.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Is.55.2	spending for what does not satisfy and listening for good food	Isaiah asks why people spend and labor for what does not satisfy, then calls them to listen and eat what is good. It binds the commentary's food-preference scene to its larger issue of whether received divine speech displaces lesser appetites.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Is.55.3	hearing, life, and an everlasting covenant	Isaiah calls hearers to incline the ear so that they may live and receive an everlasting covenant. It gives the commentary's warning-and-remembrance sequence a direct alternative in which hearing becomes enduring life.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Is.22.13	eating and drinking before death	In a prophetic crisis, people answer with eating and drinking because tomorrow they die. This is a concentrated Hebrew version of the present-pleasure orientation that the commentary contrasts with a future reckoning.
+strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 11:19	a rich person's false expectation of rest	A rich person says that there is rest and time to enjoy accumulated goods, without knowing that death will leave them to others. This Jewish wisdom scene closely mirrors the commentary's long-hope and appointed-end contrast.
+strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 6:9	Torah and deeds accompany a person after death	Rabbi Yose ben Kisma refuses a place rich in gold and jewels because, at death, neither accompanies a person except Torah and good deeds. It makes the commentary's transmission and preparation motifs a direct critique of retained wealth.
+strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 5:19	Abraham's disciples, Balaam's disciples, and the world to come	The mishnah contrasts Abraham's good eye, humility, and restrained desire with Balaam's opposite traits, assigning their disciples different ultimate destinies. It gives the commentary's Abraham pages, self-preference, high-and-low language, and final outcome a single Jewish interpretive frame.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.31.19	written song taught and placed in Israel's mouths	Moses is told to write a song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths as a witness. It closely parallels the commentary's linked scenes of written pages, recitation, remembrance, and warning.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.31.21	a song not forgotten from descendants' mouths	The song will not be forgotten from the mouths of Israel's descendants. This gives an especially close Torah counterpart to the commentary's preserved recitation and its concern that an inherited word remain available to admonish later hearers.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.15.16	little with fear of the Lord better than great treasure	Proverbs explicitly calls little with fear of the Lord better than great treasure with turmoil. Its comparative formula closely matches the commentary's claim that value, not mere temporal priority, determines what should come first.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.5.40	refusing to come for life	Jesus tells his hearers that they are unwilling to come to him in order to have life. It directly develops the commentary's distinction between access to a warning and the choice that actually turns toward life.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.21.34	hearts weighed down by the cares of life	Jesus warns that dissipation, drunkenness, and the cares of life can weigh down the heart so the day arrives suddenly. It is a close counterpart to the commentary's present-tense pattern in which near-life concerns obstruct heedfulness.
+strong	incil	motif	2 Clement 6	short fleshly sojourn and the coming age	This early homily contrasts the short residence of flesh in the present world with rest and eternal life in the coming kingdom, treating the two ages as opposed claims. It is a direct postapostolic formulation of the commentary's two-life ordering.
+strong	incil	motif	Shepherd of Hermas, Similitude 1	foreign residence and the true city	The parable treats present residence as a foreign city where possessions must be left behind when one is summoned home. It concretizes the commentary's near-life language and its refusal to mistake temporary lodging for enduring belonging.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.30.15	life and good set against death and evil	Moses sets life and good before Israel against death and evil. In its covenantal, land-centered setting it is not the same afterlife contrast, but it supplies the foundational choice-of-life formula behind the commentary's valuation of life.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.30.20	loving, obeying, and cleaving to the one who is life	Israel is to love, obey, and cleave to the Lord because he is its life and length of days. It shows that choosing life is an attachment of love and loyalty, as the commentary says preference is more than a calculation.
+medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.1.22	hearers and doers of the word	James commands hearers to become doers rather than deceive themselves by hearing alone. It offers a compact Christian formulation for the commentary's concern that the listener may know the admonition yet arrange life against it.
+medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.3.13	daily exhortation against a hardened heart	The community must exhort one another each day so that sin's deceit does not harden anyone. It matches the commentary's present-tense preference as a continually renewed condition rather than a single past decision.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Is.5.12	feasting without regard for the Lord's work	In Isaiah's woe, music and wine fill the feast while people do not regard the Lord's work. It gives a prophetic scene for the commentary's claim that near-life enjoyment can put divine reminder out of view.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.11.16	a deceived heart turning to other service	Israel is warned that its heart may be deceived and turn aside to serve other gods. It provides a covenantal analogue to the commentary's account of a foreground object displacing the right allegiance.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.8.10	instruction and knowledge above silver and gold	Wisdom tells hearers to receive instruction rather than silver and knowledge rather than fine gold. It gives the commentary's transmitted speech a concrete priority over the material goods of the near life.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hag.1.6	earning wages into a bag with holes	Haggai describes eating without satisfaction, clothing without warmth, and wages placed in a bag with holes. It supplies a vivid prophetic image for the commentary's claim that people try to hold what cannot be retained.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.2.11	labor and striving with no enduring gain	After surveying works, labor, and achievement, Qohelet finds them vapor and striving after wind with no lasting gain under the sun. It is a sapiential counterpart to the commentary's transience of what is pursued in the near life.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.18.19	Abraham's commanded legacy of righteousness and justice	Abraham is chosen so that he will command his descendants to keep the Lord's way through righteousness and justice. It gives the commentary's Abraham pages an ethical, generational content rather than merely a named ancient authority.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.3.11	Solomon choosing discernment over wealth and honor	Solomon asks for discernment instead of long life, riches, or the death of enemies. The scene gives a concrete royal counterexample to the commentary's ordering of honor, goods, and what should receive first place.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.17.11	wealth that leaves its owner before the end	Jeremiah says that wealth acquired unjustly leaves its owner in the middle of life and exposes folly at the end. It closely supports the commentary's claim that a retained worldly gain does not accompany its owner past the appointed limit.
+medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.13.17	commerce restricted by a bodily mark	Buying and selling are restricted to those bearing the beast's mark. Beside the commentary's branded-foot, visible-trace, and worldly-priority imagery, the verse makes material access a pressure to display an allegiance.
+medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Exod.16.3	Egypt's food remembered before the gift of manna	Israel remembers Egypt's flesh pots and full bread, calls death there preferable, and then receives manna. Alongside the commentary's Quranic vegetables-for-superior-provision scene, this is a related but differently framed wilderness complaint about preferring familiar food to divine provision.
